summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to assess damaged, worn or unsuitable steel fabrications and to repair, replace or modify them safely, to an agreed procedure. You will learn to find the cause of a failure, decide between repair and replacement, get the right approvals, identify the material, remove cracks and damaged parts, fit new parts and modifications, deal with galvanised steel, cast iron and worn surfaces, control distortion, inspect and test the work, keep records, and lead a small team through the job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers the **repair, replacement and modification of fabrications**: gates, grilles, frames, brackets, stands, trailers, tanks, plant parts and structural steelwork that have cracked, bent, rusted, worn out, or no longer suit the job they do.

Repair work is different from new work. The item is often dirty, rusted or painted, or still in place; nobody may know what it is made of; it may still be carrying a load; and the damage usually has a **cause** that will come back if you only weld over it. A good repair welder thinks like an inspector first and a welder second.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and welders who already make new work and now lead repair and maintenance jobs in shops, on farms, in factories and hotels, and on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Assess the damage
Make the item safe, clean and inspect all of it, find the full extent of cracks, rust and wear, and work out why it failed.
Decide what to do
Compare repair, replacement and modification on strength, cost, time and service life, and know which items you must not repair.
Agree and plan the work
Get approval from the engineer or person responsible and from the customer, price the job, and write a short repair procedure.
Make the job safe
Isolate machines, prop loads, use permits, have tanks made gas-free, deal with old coatings, and control fire and fume.
Identify the material
Use records, markings and simple workshop tests so that you choose the right filler, preheat and method.
Remove damage and prepare
Mark cut lines in sound metal, cut out damaged parts and old welds, and prepare joints to the WPS.
Repair cracks and worn parts
Find and remove cracks, weld the groove, build up worn surfaces, hardface, and repair galvanised steel and cast iron.
Fit new parts and modifications
Make replacement parts that fit, set them in line, and make changes to an agreed drawing.
Control distortion
Plan clamping, tacking and welding order, and correct distortion if it happens.
Inspect, test and hand back
Inspect visually and with crack tests, check fit and function, restore the finish, write the repair report and explain the work to the customer.
Lead the team
Brief and supervise others, set check points, and keep the job safe and recorded.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on assessing damage, repair or replace decisions, approvals, safe preparation, identifying materials, crack repair, removing parts, distortion, galvanised steel, cast iron, wear repair, modifications, inspection, records, customers and leading the job.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms or figures (for example developer, hardfacing, parent metal, bush, insert, back-step, spark test, hot work permit, as-built drawing, buffer layer, visual inspection, or a repair cost in J$) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: assess and repair cracked welded brackets, with dye penetrant checks and a repair report; and cut out and replace a damaged member of a frame, then modify the frame to a marked-up drawing.

blocks.note: Most questions at this level ask what you should do **first**, or what is **best for this job, and why**. In repair work the answer is nearly always: make it safe, find the full damage and its cause, get agreement, then weld to a procedure and check the result.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Assessing the damage and finding the cause

blocks.p: Never start a repair by welding. Start by finding out what is wrong, how far the damage goes, and why it happened. A crack that is welded over without removing its cause will usually come back, often right beside the repair.

head: Cause
What it looks like
Typical places
rows: Fatigue
A crack that grows a little with each load or vibration, often with no bending. The broken face may show curved "beach marks" spreading out from where the crack started.
Weld toes, sharp corners, holes, the ends of short welds and stiffeners, brackets on vibrating machines, trailer drawbars and spring hangers
Overload
Bending, buckling, or a torn and stretched break after one heavy load
Members loaded beyond their design; items used for a job they were not made for
Corrosion
Rust scale, pitting, thinning and holes; flaking paint with rust streaks below
Wherever water or salt sits: inside hollow sections, between lapped plates, at ground level, near the sea
Impact
Dents, bends and local cracks
Gates hit by vehicles, loader buckets, trailer sides
Wear
Metal rubbed or ground away; oval holes; thin edges
Pin holes, hinges, bucket edges, chutes, conveyor parts
Poor design or workmanship
Undersize welds, undercut, lack of fusion, welds stopped at sharp corners, the wrong material
Anywhere; often the first place to crack
Heat or fire
Scaling, sagging, warping
Items near furnaces, ovens and fires

blocks.note: Fatigue cracks usually start at a **stress raiser**: a sharp corner, a notch, undercut, an arc strike, the end of a weld, or a hole. If the repair puts the same stress raiser back, the crack will come back.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Steps in assessing a damaged item

flow: Make it safe: take it out of use, barrier it off, and take the load off or prop it
Find out the history: drawings, age, what it carries, when and how the damage was found, any earlier repairs
Clean the damaged area and the area around it to bright metal, so cracks and pits can be seen
Inspect the whole item, not only the obvious damage: other joints, fixings, hinges, the far side
Find the full length of every crack with dye penetrant (or magnetic particle testing) and mark both ends
Measure the sound metal left where there is rust or wear, and check the item for bends, twist and alignment
Identify the material, or find out how it can be identified
Decide the most likely cause, and record everything with notes, sketches and photos

ul: Rust makes steel look thicker than it is. Chip, wire-brush or grind the scale off, then measure the remaining thickness with calipers or a micrometer at the edges. An **ultrasonic thickness gauge**, where one is available, measures plate and tube walls from one side.
Measure in several places and record the thinnest. Compare it with the original thickness from the drawing or from an unworn part of the item.
For worn holes and pins, measure the diameter in two directions at right angles: the difference shows how oval the hole has become.
For frames, measure the diagonals (equal diagonals mean the frame is square), check straightness with a straight edge or string line, and check level and plumb with a spirit level.

head: Inspection aid
Use it to
rows: Good light, torch and mirror
See into inside corners, under members and behind brackets
Magnifying glass
Look closely at a possible crack
Dye penetrant kit
Show cracks that break the surface, on any non-porous metal
Magnetic particle kit (yoke and ink)
Show cracks at and just below the surface of steel (magnetic metals only)
Calipers, micrometer, ultrasonic thickness gauge
Measure how much sound metal remains
Tape, straight edge, square, string line, spirit level
Check size, alignment, squareness and twist
Camera
Record the damage before any work starts

blocks.note: Near the coast (Kingston Harbour, Montego Bay, Negril, Port Antonio and the south coast) salt air speeds up rust, most of all inside hollow sections with no drain holes, under lapped joints, and where steel stands in wet ground. Check these places on every repair, and ask whether the item has been through a hurricane, a flood or a vehicle strike.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Write down what you found before you change anything: the item and where it is; the damage (the type, size and position of each crack, thin area or bend); the likely cause; the material; and your measurements. Take photos with a rule or tape in the picture to show the size, and mark crack ends with a paint marker before you photograph them. These notes become the first part of the **repair report**.

sections.title: Deciding, agreeing and planning the work

head: Choice
When it is usually right
Points to weigh
rows: Repair
The damage is local, the metal round it is sound, the cause can be removed, and the repaired item will be as strong as it needs to be
Usually cheapest and quickest; needs skill and a procedure; may leave a weaker or shorter-lived item
Replace a part
Rust has thinned it below a safe strength, cracks are long or many, it is badly bent, or a repair would cost nearly as much as a new part
A new part of the same section and grade gives full strength and a longer life; needs accurate measuring and fitting
Replace the whole item
Damage is widespread, the design is wrong for the job, or parts cannot be had
Often the right advice for old, badly rusted gates, grilles and stands
Modify
The customer wants the item to do something new, or the design itself caused the failure (for example a sharp corner that keeps cracking)
Any change in load, balance or use is checked and approved first; the drawings are updated afterwards

blocks.p: Weigh the choices on: **safety and strength** after the work; **cost** (labour, materials, transport and the customer's downtime); **time**; how long each choice will **last**; whether the right material is available; and what the drawing, the standard or the insurer requires. Explain your advice to the customer in plain words, with the reasons, so they can decide with the facts in front of them.

blocks.note: Advising replacement when a repair would be weak is good service, not lost work. A repair that fails can hurt someone, and it costs the customer twice.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Work you must not take on alone

blocks.p: Some items are controlled by codes and laws because a failure can kill. Do not weld or patch them unless the owner has arranged for a qualified, approved repairer to work to the right code, with inspection afterwards:

ul: **Pressure equipment**: air receivers and compressor tanks, boilers, gas cylinders, LPG tanks, pressure pipework.

**Lifting equipment**: hooks, shackles, chains, crane parts, lifting beams and lugs, engine hoists. A repaired lifting item is examined, and tested where required, by a competent person before it is used again.
**Vehicle safety parts**: steering, brakes, axles, chassis rails and towing parts, where the vehicle maker's rules apply.
**Fuel tanks and containers** that have held flammable liquids, until a competent person has made them safe (see the next section).
**Structural members** of buildings and platforms, unless an engineer has designed or approved the repair.

A repair or modification to anything that carries load (a beam, column, stair, platform, lifting point or trailer drawbar) is approved **before work starts** by a qualified engineer or the person responsible for the item. They may give a drawing, a repair method, the materials and the checks.
If you need to change what was approved during the job (a different section, a moved splice, an extra cut), stop and get the change approved too.
The customer agrees the work and the price before you start, preferably in writing.

If you find more damage than you quoted for, stop, show the customer, explain the extra work and cost, and get their agreement before you carry on. Never hide damage, and never quietly add it to the bill.

blocks.p: A quotation lists the work, the price in J$, GCT at the current rate, and the time the job will take. A simple build-up of the cost:

head: Item
Example
rows: Labour
7 hours at J$2 800 an hour = J$19 600
Steel and parts
Two lengths of square hollow section and a plate = J$12 400
Consumables
Electrodes, discs, gas and paint = J$3 600
Cost before GCT
GCT
Added at the current rate

blocks.note: Compare the price of the repair with the price of a new part or item, and with how long each will last. A repair costing J$35 600 that lasts two years may be worse value than a new item at J$60 000 that lasts ten.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: For anything more than a small, simple job, write a short **repair procedure** before you start, and agree it with your supervisor, the engineer if there is one, and the customer. It makes everyone agree the steps, the checks and the safety controls before the first cut.

ul: The item, the damage found and its likely cause
What will be repaired, replaced or changed, with a sketch or the marked-up drawing
The material, the replacement sections and the filler, from the WPS or the maker's guidance
How the damage is removed and the joint prepared, and any preheat
The welding order, and how distortion will be controlled
The checks at each stage (hold points) and the final inspection and tests
The safety controls: isolation, props, permits, PPE, fire and fume
Who does each task, and who signs off
Brief the team before they start: the procedure, the hazards, each person's task, and the check points. Ask questions to make sure they have understood.
Match the task to the person: a trainee may clean, measure and prepare; a qualified welder makes the load-bearing welds, with you watching the first ones.
Set **hold points** where work stops until you have checked it: the crack fully removed, the fit-up right, the first run sound.
Watch the safety controls all through the job, not only at the start.
At the end, review the job with the team: what went well and what to do better next time.

blocks.p: Repair work brings hazards that new work does not: the item may be part of a running machine, carrying a load, full of fuel vapour, covered in old paint or zinc, or standing in a busy building. Plan the safety before you plan the welding.

flow: Agree the work with the person in charge of the machine or plant, and get the permit to work if the site uses one
Stop the machine and isolate every energy supply: electrical, hydraulic, air, steam and fuel
Lock off the isolators with your own padlock and fix a tag with your name
Release stored energy: lower raised parts or block them, bleed air and hydraulic pressure, relieve springs
Try to start the machine (or test for dead) to prove the isolation works
Only then begin; remove your lock only when the work is finished and the guards are back

blocks.note: Switching a machine off at its own switch is not isolation: someone else can switch it back on. Each person working on the machine fits their own lock.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Before you cut a member that carries load (a column, beam, stair stringer or tank stand leg), fit **temporary props** or shores that carry the load safely, and get the method approved.
Empty tanks and bins before you work on their supports.
Trailers and vehicles go on proper stands on firm ground, never on a jack alone.
A bent or twisted member can hold stored stress. When it is cut it can spring sideways, or the parts can drop. Clamp or support both sides of a cut, and stand clear of the line it could move in.

blocks.h: Tanks, drums and pipes that held flammable materials

blocks.p: Vapour left in a drum, tank or pipe that held fuel, oil, paint, solvent or chemicals can explode when it is heated, even years after it was emptied and even if it "smells clean". Rinsing it once with water is not enough. Before any heat is applied, a **competent person** must clean it (for example by steaming, or washing with the right cleaner) and prove it **gas-free** with a gas detector. Some methods also fill the container with water or an inert gas while the work is done. Follow the procedure and the competent person's written clearance.

blocks.h: Hot work in buildings and on site

ul: Get the **hot work permit** where the site uses one. It records the fire precautions, who checks them, and the fire watch.
Move anything that can burn about 10 metres or more away, or cover it with fire-resistant blankets. Look above and below for openings that sparks can fall through.
Put up screens to protect people from arc light and sparks, and barriers to keep the public away.
Keep an extinguisher of the right type at hand, with someone who knows how to use it.
Keep a **fire watch** during the work and for at least 30 minutes after it (many sites ask for 60 minutes).

Fix the work return clamp on the part being welded, close to the weld. Current that finds a path through bearings, hinges, bolts, chains, racking or a building's steel can arc and overheat at loose joints, start fires, and pit bearings.
On vehicles and machines with electronic controls, follow the maker's instructions. This usually means disconnecting the battery and protecting the control units before you weld.

head: Coating
Hazard when it is heated
Control
rows: Old paint
Fume from the paint; very old paints may contain lead
Strip it back from the weld area (often about 25 mm or more each side) with extraction; respirator as the risk assessment says
Zinc (galvanising)
Zinc oxide fume causes **metal fume fever**: flu-like chills, fever, aches and sickness a few hours later
Remove the zinc from the weld area; extraction at the arc; suitable respirator
Oil, grease, bitumen
Smoke, fire, porosity
Degrease with a non-chlorinated cleaner and let it dry
Plastic or powder coating
Irritant and toxic fume
Strip it from the weld area before heating

blocks.note: Never clean with chlorinated solvents near arc welding: the arc's ultraviolet light can turn their vapour into **phosgene**, a poisonous gas.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Work at height from a tagged scaffold, a platform or an elevating work platform, with fall protection as the site rules require.
Confined spaces (inside tanks, pits and ducts) need a permit, gas testing, ventilation and a standby person outside.
Keep your work area tidy: cables routed away from walkways, offcuts cleared, hot parts marked HOT.
Wear full welding PPE, plus a face shield and hearing protection for grinding and gouging.

blocks.p: Before you repair a part you must know, as far as you can, what it is made of. The material decides the **filler**, whether **preheat** is needed, which **process** and **method** to use, and sometimes whether the part can be welded at all. A mild steel electrode used on a high-carbon shaft or on cast iron can leave a weld that cracks as it cools.

head: Method
How it works
What it tells you
rows: Drawings, records and markings
Check the drawing, the parts list, the maker's manual, stamped or painted grade marks and mill certificates
The best source: use it whenever you can
Appearance and use
Look at the surface and shape, and ask what the part does. Castings have rough, sandy surfaces and parting lines; rolled sections have mill scale; forgings have smooth, flowing shapes.
Cast iron or cast steel, rolled steel or a forging. Springs, shafts and tools are usually higher-carbon or alloy steel.
Magnet test
Hold a magnet to a clean area

Mild and carbon steels, cast iron and some stainless steels are magnetic. **Austenitic stainless steel** (such as 304 and 316), aluminium, copper, brass and bronze are not, although austenitic stainless can be slightly magnetic where it has been bent or worked.
Spark test
Touch the part lightly to a grinding wheel and watch the sparks against a dark background
The type of steel, from the colour, length and bursts of the sparks (see the next table)
File test
Run a sharp file across an edge
A file that bites easily means soft steel; one that skids means hardened steel
Chip test
Cut a small chip with a cold chisel
Mild steel gives a smooth, continuous chip; cast iron breaks off in small, crumbly pieces
Fracture face
Look at a broken surface
Grey cast iron shows a dull grey, grainy face; steel a brighter, finer face, often torn at the edges
Weight and colour
Feel and look
Aluminium is light and pale; copper alloys are red or yellow
Analysis
A spot-test kit or a hand-held analyser where available, or a laboratory test
The actual composition, for load-bearing and pressure work

head: Material
Typical sparks
rows: Mild (low-carbon) steel
Long, straw-yellow streams with a few small forks or bursts
Medium- and high-carbon steel
Shorter, brighter streams with many bushy, star-like bursts; the more carbon, the more bursts
Grey cast iron
Short, dull red-orange streams with small bursts close to the wheel
Stainless steel
Shorter, orange to straw streams with few or no bursts
Aluminium, copper, brass
Few or no sparks

blocks.note: Spark testing takes practice. Keep a set of labelled sample bars (mild steel, high-carbon steel, cast iron and stainless) and compare the part's sparks with theirs on the same wheel. Wear eye protection and keep the sparks away from anything that can burn.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: If you cannot identify the material of a load-bearing part, do not guess. Have it tested, or ask the engineer to decide. If a decision must be made on the spot, treat it as the harder-to-weld material: for example, use preheat and low-hydrogen filler as for a medium-carbon steel.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Material
Where you meet it
What it means for the repair
rows: Mild steel
Gates, grilles, frames, stands, most brackets
Easy to weld; use a matching filler (for example E7018 or E6013 electrodes, or ER70S-6 wire)
Medium- and high-carbon steel
Shafts, axles, pins, springs, blades, rails
Hardens and cracks next to the weld; needs preheat, low-hydrogen filler and slow cooling, to a procedure. Springs and heat-treated tools are usually replaced, not welded.
High-strength steel
Truck chassis, crane parts, wear plate
Follow the maker's repair instructions; some may not be welded or heated at all
Cast iron
Pump bodies, gearbox and motor housings, old machine parts, manhole frames
Brittle; cracks from heat stress; needs special filler and method
Stainless steel
Food equipment, kitchen frames, tanks, fittings
Needs stainless filler and its own clean tools; usually GTAW, GMAW or stainless MMAW electrodes
Aluminium
Boat parts, truck bodies, ladders, signs
Needs GTAW or GMAW with aluminium filler and argon; heat-treated alloys lose strength near the weld
Galvanised steel
Fencing, grilles, rails, farm gates, structural steel
Remove the zinc from the weld area, control the fume, and restore the coating

sections.title: Removing damage, preparing joints and fitting new parts

ul: Measure and record the item's key sizes **before** you cut: lengths, centres, diagonals, heights and hole positions. You need them to set the new part.
Mark cut lines in **sound metal**, beyond the end of the rust, crack or bend, so that only the damage is removed and the new piece meets good steel.
Mark the lines square to the member (use a wrap-around strip for tube and pipe), and add centre lines and match marks across the cut so the new part can be lined up.
Keep new butt joints clear of existing welds, holes and bends and of the points of highest load, or where the engineer directs.

blocks.h: Choosing how to cut and remove

head: Method
Best for
Points to watch
rows: Abrasive cut-off disc (grinder)
Small sections, tube, cutting close to other parts
Little heat; guard on; disc rated for the grinder's speed; sparks controlled
Saw (bandsaw, hacksaw, portable saw)
Clean, square cuts with no heat
Slow on heavy sections; the part must be clamped
Oxy-fuel cutting
Thick carbon steel; fast site cutting
Wide heat-affected zone; does not cut stainless steel, aluminium or cast iron; grind off the oxide before welding
Plasma cutting
Any metal that conducts, thin to medium
Fast, narrow cut; fume and noise; needs power and compressed air
Air carbon arc gouging
Removing old welds, cracks and backing; back-gouging
Very fast; loud and smoky; leaves a carbon-rich surface that must be ground back to bright metal before welding
Grinding
Short cracks, small welds, dressing
Slow but very controlled
Drilling
Crack stop holes; removing rivets and spot welds
Centre-punch first; clamp the work

blocks.h: Removing an old part without damaging the main member

ul: Remove the **weld**, not the parent metal: gouge or grind the old fillet away, stopping when you reach the surface of the main plate.
Do not hammer the part off, and do not heat the whole member red hot to pull it off: both damage the main member and can start cracks.
Dress the surface flush and check it with dye penetrant for any cracks the old part may have started.

Prepare the ends for the weld that the drawing or WPS asks for. A **full-strength butt weld** in thicker material usually needs a bevel: for example, for MMAW on plate, a single-V with about a 60° included angle, a root face of about 1–2 mm and a root gap of about 2–3 mm. The WPS gives the exact figures.
Hollow sections cannot be welded from the inside, so a splice in tube is often made on a **backing strip** or an internal backing sleeve that lets the root fuse fully from the outside.
Clean every joint face, and about 25 mm each side of it, to bright metal: rust, scale, paint, zinc, oil and old slag all cause defects.
Grind off the carbon-rich layer left by gouging and the oxide left by flame cutting.
Use the **same section, size, thickness and grade** as the original unless the engineer approves a change. A thinner or smaller section may be easier to weld in, but it makes a weak point.
Check the grade from the drawing, the supplier's markings or the mill certificate.
A length of new section welded into a member in place of a damaged length is called an **insert** or a **splice**.

blocks.h: Making a replacement part when there is no drawing

flow: Measure the old part fully, including holes, centres and fixing points; measure an unworn area if the part is worn
Measure the mating parts and the space the part fits into, as they may differ from the old part
Sketch the part with all its sizes, and check the sketch against the job
For awkward shapes, make a template in card or thin sheet and offer it up
Make the part, check it against the sketch, and trial-fit it before final welding

ul: Clamp and tack the new part, then check its alignment in **both directions**, its level or plumb, and the item's squareness (diagonals) before full welding. Tacks are easy to break and re-set; full welds are not.
Make tacks with the same filler and care as the final weld: they become part of it.
On frames, tack every new joint first, check the whole frame, then weld in the planned order.

blocks.p: A modification changes what an item is or does: a door cut into a grille, a ramp added to a trailer, an extra bracket on a frame, a hoist beam fixed to a structure. Before you agree to one, check:

ul: **Strength and load**: will the change add load, move load onto another member, or remove material that was carrying load?
**Balance**: will it move the centre of gravity, or change the weight on a hitch or an axle?
**Function and clearance**: will doors still swing, parts still move and people still get past?
**Approval**: who must approve it (the engineer, the owner, the vehicle maker)?
**Drawings**: make or mark up a drawing of the change and agree it before you start. When the job is finished, mark the drawing **as built**, so later repairs work from what is really there.

sections.title: Repairing cracks and testing for them

blocks.p: A crack has a sharp tip where stress gathers. Each time the part is loaded, the tip can grow a little further. That is why a crack must be found to its ends, removed completely and replaced with sound weld metal. Welding over a crack leaves a hidden notch under the weld that will grow again.

Penetrant testing shows cracks and pores that break the surface, on any metal that is not porous. A kit has three aerosol cans: **cleaner (remover)**, **penetrant** (usually red) and **developer** (white).

flow: Clean the surface to bare metal, removing all paint, scale, oil and grinding dust, and let it dry
Spray penetrant over the area and leave it for the dwell time on the can (often about 10–20 minutes)
Wipe off the surface penetrant with a dry, lint-free cloth, then with a cloth dampened with cleaner. Do not spray cleaner straight onto the area: it washes the penetrant out of the cracks
Spray a thin, even coat of developer from about 30 cm and leave it for the time on the can
Inspect in good light: red lines on the white show cracks; red dots show pores
Mark the ends of each indication, record and photograph it, then clean the area

blocks.note: Penetrant products are flammable and give off vapour. Use them with ventilation, away from arcs and sparks, wearing gloves, and as the safety data sheet (SDS) says. Dispose of empty cans as the SDS and the Centre's rules say.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: MT works only on magnetic metals such as carbon steel. A yoke magnetises the area, and fine iron particles (in a spray or as a powder) gather where a crack disturbs the magnetic field. It finds cracks at the surface and just below it, even through a thin coat of paint. Test in two directions at right angles, because a crack shows best when it lies across the field. A trained operator does it.

flow: Take the load off or prop the part; get the approvals and permits needed
Clean to bright metal, find both ends of the crack with PT or MT, and mark them
If the procedure says, drill a small **stop hole** just beyond each end of the crack, to stop it running while you work
Identify the material, and take the filler, preheat and settings from the WPS or the maker's guidance
Remove the crack completely by grinding or gouging, shaping a U or V groove with sloping sides and a rounded bottom
Check the groove with PT; if any red line shows, remove more metal and check again
Preheat if required, then weld the groove in clean runs, removing slag between runs and keeping the heat even
Fill the stop holes if the procedure says, and dress the weld smooth, with no sharp notches or undercut
When the part has cooled, inspect it visually and with PT or MT, then record the repair

blocks.note: For a crack right through a plate, gouge from one side to about half way, weld that side, then back-gouge from the other side until you reach sound weld metal, and weld again. Both sides are then fully fused, like a double-V joint.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Some procedures ask you to wait a set time (for example a day) after welding before the final crack test on thick or hardenable steel, because hydrogen cracks can appear hours after the weld has cooled.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: A reinforcing plate (a doubler or fish plate) adds strength where the engineer asks for it. Give it **rounded corners** or tapered ends, so that the stiffness changes gradually.
Do not start or stop welds at a sharp corner, where they leave a stress point; carry the weld round the corner.
Do not put the toe of a reinforcing weld on top of a repaired crack, and never use a plate to cover a crack that has not been removed.
Keep weld profiles smooth: on parts that vibrate, a smooth, blended weld toe lasts much longer than a sharp one.

head: Test
What it finds
Notes
rows: Visual inspection (VT)
Surface defects, size, shape, alignment
Always first; needs good light, a mirror and gauges
Penetrant testing (PT)
Surface-breaking cracks and pores
Any non-porous metal
Magnetic particle testing (MT)
Cracks at and just below the surface
Magnetic metals only
Ultrasonic testing (UT)
Internal defects; remaining wall thickness
Trained operator; good for cracks and lack of fusion inside a weld
Radiography (RT)
Internal porosity, slag and lack of penetration
Radiation safety rules; trained, licensed operators

sections.title: Galvanised steel, cast iron and wear repair

ul: Grind or flap-disc the zinc off the weld area, on both faces, for a short distance each side of the joint (often about 25 mm, or as the procedure says). Zinc in the weld causes porosity and cracking.
Use extraction at the arc and the respirator the risk assessment names. Never weld galvanised steel in a closed space without them.

After welding, remove slag and spatter and restore the corrosion protection over all bare steel, overlapping onto the sound zinc: **zinc-rich paint** (cold galvanising), zinc metal spray, or the method the specification gives, applied to clean, dry steel to the thickness on the data sheet.

blocks.note: Weld metal and bare steel rust quickly outdoors, and in salt air they can show rust within days. Restoring the coating is part of the repair, not an extra.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Grey cast iron contains flakes of graphite that make it brittle. When one part of a casting is heated and the rest stays cold, the stress can crack it, and the metal next to the weld can become very hard and brittle. Repair methods either keep the heat low and local, or make the whole casting hot and cool it very slowly.

head: Step
Cold method (common for small repairs)
Hot method (specialist work)
rows: Preparation
Find the crack ends, drill stop holes, grind a U groove; heat the area gently to burn out oil that has soaked into the iron
The same, plus a furnace or careful heating of the whole casting
Filler
Nickel or nickel-iron electrodes (nickel-iron is stronger, for heavier sections), as the procedure says
Cast-iron filler, or as the procedure says
Heat
Little or no preheat; keep the casting near the weld no hotter than you can touch
Preheat the whole casting evenly to the high temperature the procedure sets
Welding
Short runs (often about 25–50 mm), spread out in a skip order; peen each run lightly with a round-nosed hammer while it is hot; let it cool to hand-warm before the next
Weld while the casting is hot
Cooling
Slowly, in still air, away from draughts
Very slowly, wrapped or in the furnace

blocks.note: Braze welding with bronze and mechanical stitching are other ways to repair cast iron with less heat. Do not try to cut cast iron with an oxy-fuel torch: it does not cut cleanly. Grind or saw it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Worn pin holes and bores** are built up with weld and then bored or reamed back to size and position, or bored oversize and fitted with a pressed-in **bush** (a short tube) that brings the hole back to size and can be replaced when it wears.
**Worn shafts and pins** can be built up with weld and machined, but they are often medium-carbon steel: preheat and use low-hydrogen filler as the procedure says, or replace them.
Do not fill a worn hole with body filler, and do not fit a bigger pin in an oval hole: the wear carries on, faster.

blocks.p: **Hardfacing** is a weld deposit laid on a surface to make it resist wear: bucket edges and teeth, crusher parts, plough points, chutes, conveyor scrapers and cane-cutting knives. The filler is a special alloy, often rich in chromium carbides, that is much harder than the part.

flow: Clean the worn area, check the base metal for cracks, and identify it (manganese steel and carbon steel need different methods)
If it is badly worn, build it back towards shape with a tough build-up filler
Lay a **buffer layer** first if the maker says, to bond well to the base and stop cracks in the hard layer running into the part
Lay the hardfacing in the pattern the maker advises (stringer beads, a cross-hatch or waffle, or dots), in no more layers than the maker allows
Let it cool as the maker says, then inspect it

blocks.note: Many hard chromium-carbide deposits form fine cracks straight across the bead as they cool, called **relief cracks** or **check cracks**. These are normal for those fillers and relieve stress. A crack that runs along the bead, or down into the base metal, is not normal.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Use a filler that matches or suits the parent metal (for example ER308L or ER316L for those stainless steels, or the maker's aluminium filler), with the process and gas the WPS gives.
Keep separate brushes, discs and clamps for stainless steel and aluminium: carbon steel particles cause rust spots on stainless.
Heat-treated aluminium alloys lose strength near a weld; get engineering advice before repairing load-bearing aluminium.

blocks.p: Weld metal and the steel beside it expand as they heat and **shrink** as they cool, pulling the parts towards the weld. Repairs often add weld to one side of a member, or are made on a frame that is already fixed in place, so the pull is uneven and stresses are locked in. The more weld metal and heat, the more distortion.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Clamps, braces or strongbacks
Hold the parts in line while the weld cools
Even tacking, checked before welding
Sets the parts right while they can still be moved
Pre-setting
Sets the parts slightly the opposite way, so the shrinkage pulls them straight
Balanced welding
Welds opposite sides of a joint or member in turn, so the pulls cancel out
Back-step welding
Welds short lengths in the opposite direction to the overall progress, so heat is spread and shrinkage does not build up one way
Skip (intermittent) sequence
Welds short lengths spread along the joint, then fills the gaps
The smallest weld that does the job
Less weld metal, less shrinkage: never over-weld
Cooling between runs
Stops heat building up in one area

ul: Measure first (diagonals, straightness and level) and record the readings.
**Mechanical correction:** pull or push the part back with clamps, a jack or a press, in small steps, checking as you go.

**Heat straightening:** heat small spots, lines or wedge shapes on the long (outer) side of the bend; as they cool they shrink and pull the member back. For mild steel keep to a dull red at most (about 600–650 °C), let it cool in air, and never quench it with water. Some high-strength steels must not be heat-straightened at all, so check first.
Check again after each step, and record the final readings.

head: Check
How
rows: Weld quality
Visual inspection with good light, a mirror and a magnifier: no cracks, undercut, porosity, overlap or lack of fusion; slag and spatter removed
Weld size and profile
Fillet or weld gauge, against the drawing or procedure; a smooth blend at the toes
Cracks
PT or MT, where the procedure asks or the part carries load
Dimensions and alignment
Tape, square, straight edge, diagonals and level, against the drawing and your first measurements
Function
Gates swing freely and latch; hinges and pins move; bolts line up; loads sit correctly
Fitness for service
Lifting and load-bearing items are examined, and tested where required, by a competent person before they are used again

blocks.note: Never "test" a repair by loading it until it bends, or by hanging on a load nobody has set. A load test is planned, done to a set test load with people kept clear, and recorded by a competent person.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Remove slag, spatter and sharp edges, and dress welds where the drawing asks.
Clean to the standard the paint maker's data sheet asks for, then prime (zinc-rich primer on galvanised or outdoor steel) and top-coat as specified, in a ventilated area, with the PPE the SDS names.
Paint the inside of hollow sections where you can, and make sure drain holes are clear.

blocks.p: The **repair report** is the written record of the job. Keep a copy in the job file and give one to the customer. It should include:

ul: The customer, the item, its location and the date
The damage found and its likely cause, with measurements
The decision (repair, replace or modify) and who approved it
The method, the materials and filler, the WPS used, and who did the welding
The inspection and test results
Photos taken before, during and after the work
Advice: care, painting, when to inspect again, and anything still to watch
Marked-up (as-built) drawings for any modification
Label any damaged part that must be kept for investigation or that the customer wants back; put the rest in the scrap metal bin for recycling. Never leave offcuts on the floor.
Leave the area clean. Remove barriers and close permits only when the area is safe, and remove your lock last.
Show the customer the work, explain what was done and why, give them the report and any care advice, and check that the invoice matches what was agreed.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can make a damaged item safe, inspect all of it, and find the full extent of the damage.
I can name the common causes of failure (fatigue, overload, corrosion, impact, wear, poor design or workmanship) and recognise the signs of each.
I can measure the sound metal left in a rusted or worn part, and check a frame for square, straightness and twist.
I can compare repair, replacement and modification, and explain my advice to a customer.
I can name the items I must not repair without approved people and a code (pressure, lifting, vehicle safety, fuel containers, structure).
I can get the approvals a load-bearing job needs, and deal correctly with extra damage found during a job.
I can price a repair in J$ and write a short repair procedure.
I can isolate and lock off a machine, prop a load, and set up hot work safely.
I can identify common materials with records, a magnet, a spark test, a file test and a chip test.
I can mark cut lines in sound metal, choose a cutting method, and remove an old part without damaging the main member.
I can prepare a joint, choose replacement material, and make a replacement part without a drawing.
I can carry out a dye penetrant test and explain magnetic particle testing.
I can repair a crack step by step, including stop holes, grooving, checking and welding.
I can repair galvanised steel and cast iron, build up worn holes, and hardface a worn edge.
I can prevent, measure and correct distortion.
I can inspect a repair, restore the finish, write a repair report, and hand the job back.
I can brief and lead a small repair team and set hold points.

terms: As-built drawing
A drawing marked up after a job to show what was actually built or changed
Back-gouging
Removing metal from the back of a weld to reach sound metal before welding that side
Back-step welding
Welding short lengths in the opposite direction to the overall progress of the weld, to reduce distortion
Buffer layer
A tough weld layer laid under hardfacing to help it bond and to stop cracks running into the part
Bush
A short tube pressed into a worn hole to bring it back to size
Check cracks
Fine cracks across a hardfacing bead that form on cooling; normal for many hard alloys
Competent person
Someone with the training, knowledge and experience to do a task, such as declaring a tank gas-free or examining lifting equipment
Developer
The white spray in a penetrant test that draws the dye out of a crack so it can be seen
Fatigue
Cracking caused by repeated loads or vibration, often at a stress raiser
Gas-free
Proved by a competent person, with a gas detector, to hold no flammable vapour
Hardfacing
A weld deposit laid on a surface to make it resist wear
Heat straightening
Correcting distortion with controlled local heating that shrinks the metal back
Hold point
A stage at which work stops until it has been checked and approved
Hot work permit
A written permit to weld, cut or grind where there is a fire risk
Insert (splice)
A new length of section welded in place of a damaged length
Isolation (lock-off)
Cutting off and locking every energy supply to a machine before work on it
Magnetic particle testing (MT)
A crack test for magnetic metals using a magnet and fine iron particles
Metal fume fever
Flu-like illness caused by breathing zinc or other metal oxide fume
Modification
A change to what an item is or does
Parent metal
The original metal of the part, as opposed to the weld metal; also called base metal
Peening
Lightly hammering a weld run while hot to relieve shrinkage stress
Penetrant testing (PT)
A crack test using a coloured dye, a cleaner and a developer
Preheat
Warming the parent metal before welding to slow cooling and reduce cracking
Repair procedure
The written, agreed steps, materials, checks and safety controls for a repair
Repair report
The record of the damage found, the method, the materials and the checks made
Spark test
Identifying a steel by the colour and shape of its sparks on a grinder
Stop hole
A small hole drilled just past the end of a crack to stop it running
Stress raiser
A sharp change in shape, such as a corner, notch or undercut, where cracks start
Visual inspection
Checking a weld or repair by eye, with light, a mirror and gauges
Zinc-rich paint
A paint with a high zinc content, used to restore protection on galvanised steel

c1.title: A cracked pump bracket in Bath
c1.text: Shanique, a Level 3 welder, leads a two-person crew sent to a water pumping station in Bath, St Thomas. A welded bracket of 12 mm mild steel plate holds a pump motor. A crack about 70 mm long runs from the toe of a fillet weld at a sharp inside corner, with rust streaks below it. The motor vibrates when it runs. The station's supervisor asks the crew to "just run a bead over it" while the pump keeps running, because the town's water depends on it.

c2.title: Rusted balcony posts in Oracabessa
c2.text: A guest house by the sea in Oracabessa, St Mary, has galvanised balcony rails with 48 mm round tube posts welded to base plates. At the foot of four posts the tube has rusted through just above the base-plate weld: rain water has been sitting inside the posts, which have no drain holes. The owner asks Kemar, a Level 3 welder, to "weld some plates over the holes" before the tourist season. Kemar's trainee, Rushane, will help.

c3.title: A hoist beam for a store in Brown's Town
c3.text: A hardware store in Brown's Town, St Ann, wants a 1-tonne chain hoist on a new steel beam fixed under the roof frame of its storeroom, to lift cement off trucks. Damion, who runs a small fabrication shop, has been asked to quote. The store manager says the roof steel "looks strong enough" and does not want to pay for an engineer. The storeroom holds paint, cardboard boxes and steel shelving.

c4.title: Worn and broken parts at a quarry near Duncans
c4.text: Tyrone leads the maintenance welders at a limestone quarry near Duncans, Trelawny. This week he has three jobs: the cutting edge of a loader bucket is worn thin; a lug has cracked off the housing of a conveyor gearbox; and a crusher drive pin about 50 mm across has a worn section that the fitter wants built up with weld. The broken face of the gearbox lug is dull grey and grainy, and a chisel only breaks small, crumbly chips from it.

c5.title: A security grille in Lucea
c5.text: At a pharmacy in Lucea, Hanover, a reversing van bent the bottom rail and two bars of a steel security grille made of 25 mm square tube. Natasha leads two trainees on the repair. Before cutting, she measured the frame's diagonals: 1 846 mm and 1 849 mm. The new bottom rail was then fully welded at one end before the other end was tacked, and afterwards the diagonals measured 1 838 mm and 1 857 mm. The old paint on the grille is thick and flaking.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the crack in the bracket?
o: Fatigue from vibration, starting at the sharp corner
Rust from the damp sea air slowly thinning the plate
One heavy overload when the motor was first lifted in
Shrinkage of the weld metal when the bracket was made
questions.why: A crack that starts at a weld toe at a sharp corner on a vibrating part, with no bending, is typical fatigue. The rust streaks show the crack has been open for some time, not that rust caused it.

questions.q: How should Shanique answer the supervisor's request?
o: Weld it now as asked, and come back next week to do a proper repair
Weld it running, but with low current so the motor is not harmed
Explain it must be stopped, isolated and its load supported first
Weld it running, with the work clamp fixed on the motor's frame
questions.why: Welding a running, vibrating machine is unsafe, and a bead over a crack leaves the crack under the weld. The pump is isolated and locked off and the bracket's load taken off or propped; the station arranges the shutdown, perhaps with a standby pump.

questions.q: Shanique sprays penetrant, waits, then sprays cleaner straight onto the area to wash the red off before applying developer. Only part of the crack shows. What went wrong?
o: The developer went on before the dwell time ended
The cleaner washed penetrant out of the crack
The penetrant needs a hot surface to work well
The crack is too fine for any penetrant to enter
questions.why: Excess penetrant is wiped off with a dry cloth, then with a cloth dampened with cleaner. Spraying cleaner straight on flushes penetrant out of the crack, so the indication is weak or missing; the test must be done again from clean.

questions.q: The crack has been ground out into a U groove. What shows that the groove is ready to be welded?
o: The groove looks bright and clean along its full length
The groove has been ground as deep as the crack first looked
Tapping it with a hammer gives a clear, ringing sound
A second penetrant check of the groove shows no red line
questions.why: A crack can run deeper or further than it first looks. Only a fresh penetrant (or magnetic particle) check that shows no indication proves it has all gone; any red line means more grinding and another check.

questions.q: Apart from removing and re-welding the crack, which change does most to stop it coming back?
o: Making the new weld larger than the old one so it is stronger
Replacing the sharp corner with a smooth radius or gusset
Painting the repair with two coats of red oxide primer
Welding the groove in one heavy run at a high current
questions.why: Fatigue cracks start at stress raisers such as sharp corners and abrupt weld toes. Removing the stress raiser deals with the cause, with the change agreed by the person responsible; a bigger weld or paint leaves the cause in place.

questions.q: What should Kemar advise the owner?
o: Weld plates over the holes, since the posts will then look sound again
Fill the holes up with weld metal and then paint the posts silver
Cut out the rusted length and splice in new tube of the same size
Cover the holes with fibreglass and resin, which can never rust
questions.why: Plates welded over rotten tube are joined to thin, rusty metal and leave the rot inside, and a balcony rail is a safety barrier. Cutting back to sound metal and splicing in matching tube restores its strength.

questions.q: Before he cuts the first post, what should Kemar do?
o: Cut through all four posts together so the rail settles evenly
Heat the posts red hot first so the rusty part pulls away easily
Knock the rusted feet off with a sledgehammer to save time
Record the post positions and rail height, and prop the rail
questions.why: Once the posts are cut, the rail is unsupported, and it must end up at the same height and line. Measuring first and propping the rail keeps everyone safe and lets the new lengths be set exactly.

questions.q: Which change would help the new post feet last longer?
o: Seal the post tops or drill small drain holes at the foot
Fill the bottom of each post with dry sand before it is welded
Use much larger fillet welds where the posts meet the plates
Paint just the outside of the posts with a thick gloss paint
questions.why: The posts rotted from the inside because rain water collected in them. Keeping water out, or letting it drain at the foot, removes the cause; sand holds moisture against the steel and makes rust worse.

questions.q: That evening Rushane has chills, aches and a fever, like flu. He spent the afternoon grinding and welding the galvanised posts in a corner with no air movement. What is the most likely cause?
o: Arc eye from light reflected off the rails
Metal fume fever from breathing zinc fume
Heat exhaustion from working in the afternoon sun
A slight electric shock through his sweaty gloves
questions.why: Heated zinc gives off zinc oxide fume, which causes flu-like metal fume fever a few hours later. Remove the zinc from the weld area and use extraction and a respirator; Rushane should report it and get medical advice.

questions.q: What should Damion tell the manager?
o: He can fit it if he uses a heavier beam than the roof needs
An engineer must check the roof and approve the design first
He can fit it once the manager signs to take the responsibility
He can fit it if the hoist is only used for half its rated load
questions.why: A lifting load hung from a roof frame adds load the frame may not have been designed for. A qualified engineer must check the structure and approve the beam and fixings; a signature or a heavier beam does not make an overloaded roof safe.

questions.q: Halfway through the job, Damion finds a light fitting in the way and wants to fix the beam 600 mm from where the approved drawing shows it. What should he do?
o: Move it, as 600 mm will make no real difference to the roof
Move it, and mark the new position on the drawing afterwards
Get the engineer's approval for the new position first
Leave it as drawn and let the hoist chain rub on the light
questions.why: Moving the beam moves the load to a part of the roof the engineer has not checked. Any change to an approved design is approved before it is made; the drawing is then marked up as built.

questions.q: Why should the work return clamp go on the new beam close to the weld, and not on the store's steel shelving?
o: Stray current through shelving bolts can arc and start fires
The shelving steel is far too thin to carry welding current
The clamp would scratch the paint on the store's shelving
The machine's open-circuit voltage rises when it passes through shelving
questions.why: Welding current takes every path back to the machine. Through bolted shelving, hinges or bearings it can arc and overheat at loose joints, here among paint and cardboard. The clamp goes on the part being welded, close to the joint.

questions.q: Damion allows 9 hours of labour at J$3 200 an hour, J$38 500 for the beam and fixings, and J$4 700 for consumables. What is the price before GCT?
questions.why: Labour is 9 × J$3 200 = J$28 800. Then J$28 800 + J$38 500 + J$4 700 = J$72 000. GCT is added at the current rate.

questions.q: Before anyone uses the new hoist beam, what must it be marked with?
o: Its safe working load, once tested and examined
The fabricator's name and telephone number for repairs
The date it was painted and the colour code of the paint
The weight of the beam itself, for whoever takes it down
questions.why: Lifting equipment is examined, and proof-tested where required, by a competent person, and clearly marked with its safe working load (SWL) so nobody overloads it. The test record is kept.

questions.q: What is the gearbox housing most likely made of?
o: Mild steel plate
Grey cast iron
Austenitic stainless steel
Aluminium alloy
questions.why: A dull grey, grainy fracture and crumbly chips are signs of grey cast iron, which is common for gearbox and pump housings. It needs a cast-iron method, such as nickel electrodes, short peened runs and slow cooling.

questions.q: A spark test on the crusher pin gives short, bright streams full of bushy, star-like bursts. What should Tyrone conclude?
o: It is mild steel, so any general electrode will do
It is stainless steel, so it needs a stainless filler
It is cast iron, so it must be brazed and not welded
It is higher-carbon steel and needs a set procedure
questions.why: Many bright, bushy bursts show high carbon. Such steel hardens and cracks next to a weld, so it needs preheat, low-hydrogen filler and slow cooling to a procedure, or the pin is replaced.

questions.q: After the bucket edge is hardfaced, fine cracks run straight across each bead but stop at the buffer layer. What should Tyrone do?
o: Grind off all the hardfacing and lay it again at a higher current
Fill each crack with mild steel weld before the bucket is used
Accept them if the maker says such check cracks are normal
Reject the bucket, as any crack in hardfacing means it will fail
questions.why: Many chromium-carbide hardfacing alloys form cross-cracks as they cool, which relieve stress and are expected. Cracks that run along the bead or down into the base metal are not normal and must be investigated.

questions.q: What do Natasha's two sets of diagonal readings show?
o: The frame was twisted before, and is now flat and square
The frame was square before, and is now out of square
The frame has grown longer because the new rail stretched it
Both readings are within a few millimetres, so all is well
questions.why: Equal diagonals mean a rectangle is square. A 3 mm difference before the work was close to square; 19 mm afterwards shows the frame has been pulled into a parallelogram by the shrinkage of the rail welds.

questions.q: Which way of working would most likely have kept the grille square?
o: Tack all joints, check square, then weld in balanced order
Weld each joint fully in turn, starting from the left side
Weld at the highest current so each joint is done quickly
Weld one side of every joint, then cool them all with water
questions.why: Tacking every joint first and checking the diagonals sets the frame square while it can still be adjusted; welding opposite sides and corners in turn balances the shrinkage. Water does not stop shrinkage and can crack some steels.

questions.q: The old paint is thick and flaking and may be decades old. How should the team deal with it at the joints?
o: Let the welding arc burn it off as they weld along each joint
Wash it down with a chlorinated degreaser before they weld
Paint over it with a primer so that the paint stops flaking off
Strip it from the joints, with extraction and a respirator
questions.why: Burning paint gives off harmful fume, very old paint may contain lead, and it spoils the weld. Remove it from the weld area with extraction and the respirator the risk assessment names; chlorinated solvents can form phosgene near the arc.
